spots.rule: G + i, a front vowel: the Swedish j sound, so it starts like yillar.
Skj is always the sj sound, even before o.
Sk + ö, a front vowel: the sj sound.
Å is the real O: deep and round. A single r follows, so stretch it.
The same deep, round å as in från.
K + i, a front vowel: the soft tj sound.
Å followed by one n: a long, round å.

Use och before the last language. Put lite directly before a language you speak only a little.

activity.pattern: Many language names end in -ska: finska, svenska, ryska, tyska, turkiska, kinesiska, portugisiska, engelska. Countries take a capital letter; languages do not. Hindi, urdu and bengali keep their own names, and the language is hindi, not hindu.

sections.title: Nine vowels: copy the mouth first
body: Swedish has nine vowel letters: A, O, U, Y, I, E, Ö, Ä, Å. First copy the lip and tongue position; then copy the audio.
English, Hindi, and Marathi examples are memory bridges, not exact Swedish pronunciation. The Swedish recording is the final model.
Rounded lips: O, U, Y, Ö, Å. Front tongue: I, E, Y, Ä, Ö. Notice that Y and Ö belong to both groups.

examples.fi: jag · ja · bok · bor
examples.en: A and O lesson words
examples.note: Open for A; round for O.

examples.fi: dum · du · paraply · by
examples.en: U and Y lesson words
examples.note: Keep the lips rounded; move the tongue forward for Y.

examples.fi: Indien · le · ö · bär · från
examples.en: I, E, Ö, Ä, and Å lesson words
examples.note: Compare the mouth shapes; do not force an English sound.

activity.label: Mouth map
activity.title: Explore the nine vowels one mouth at a time
activity.instructions: Tap a vowel, copy the mouth cue, and hear its lesson words. Then light up a group to see which vowels share a mouth shape.

features.label: Rounded lips
features.note: O, U, Y, Ö and Å push the lips forward into a circle. Check in a mirror.

features.label: Front vowels
features.note: E, I, Y, Ä and Ö keep the tongue forward. Remember this group: it softens g, k and sk in topic 4.

sounds.cue: Open wide and let the sound sit at the back of the mouth. आ is a starting bridge.
Round the lips as in boots. In these words Swedish O sounds close to a long oo.
Tight rounded lips, as if drinking through a straw. Long u in du and short u in dum sound different: copy each one.
Say I, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for U.
Wide smile, tongue high and forward. ई is a starting bridge.
A lighter smile than I. ए is a starting bridge.
Say E, keep the tongue still, and round the lips as for O.
Drop the jaw as for A, but aim for E. Near the e in bed.
The real O: deep and round. ऑ or English aw is a starting bridge.

contrasts.label: I → Y
contrasts.audio: i, y. i, y. Kina, by.
contrasts.cue: Tongue stays still. Only the lips round.

contrasts.label: E → Ö
contrasts.audio: e, ö. e, ö. le, ö.
contrasts.cue: Same trick: keep the E tongue, round the lips.

contrasts.label: O → Å
contrasts.cue: Swedish O often sounds like oo. The O you know from English is usually written Å.

sections.title: Long or short: stretch one part
body: In a stressed Swedish syllable, either the vowel is long or the consonant after it is long. Hear both parts, not only the vowel.

A common spelling clue is: one consonant letter after the stressed vowel often means a longer vowel; a doubled consonant often means a short vowel and longer consonant. It is a clue, not a rule without exceptions.
Use the routine: find the stressed vowel → look right → listen → copy the whole word.

examples.fi: tak — tack
examples.en: roof — thanks
examples.note: Stretch the a in tak; stop it quickly and hold the k in tack.

examples.fi: kafé — kaffe
examples.en: café — coffee
examples.note: Hear the stressed final é in kafé and the short a plus long f in kaffe.

examples.fi: bor — mamma · pappa · pluggar
examples.en: lives — mum · dad · studies
examples.note: Bor has a long stressed vowel; the doubled consonants signal short stressed vowels in the other words.

rows: cut the vowel; hold the consonant

sections.memoryTip: Single often means STRETCH. Double often means STOP the vowel quickly—but always check the stressed syllable and listen.
sections.tryIt: Say tak—tack three times. Make the contrast bigger than feels natural, then say the pair normally.

activity.label: Stretch or stop?
activity.title: Predict the length from the spelling, then check by ear
activity.instructions: Look at the highlighted stressed vowel and the letters after it. Choose stretch or stop, then play the word to confirm.

buckets.label: Stretch
buckets.hint: long vowel · one consonant after it

buckets.label: Stop
buckets.hint: short vowel · two consonants after it

items.why: One k after the a: stretch the a.
ck counts as a double consonant: cut the a and hold the k.
One k after the o: stretch it.
Double f: a short a and a long f.
One r after the o: stretch it.
Double m: stop the a quickly and hold the m.
Nothing follows the stressed y, so it is long.
Double p: short a, long p.
One n after the å: stretch it.
Double t: short ö, long t.
Two different consonants, s and t, also usually mean a short vowel.
Double g after the stressed u: keep the u short.

activity.summary: One consonant after the stressed vowel usually means stretch. Two consonants usually mean stop. It is a strong clue, not a law, so the recording always has the final say.

sections.title: One vowel group, three soft sounds
body: The spelling group E, I, Y, Ä, Ö often softens the consonant immediately before it. These are front vowels because the tongue is forward; Y and Ö still use rounded lips.
G usually becomes the Swedish j sound, K usually becomes the tj sound /ɕ/, and SK usually becomes the sj sound /ɧ/ before this group.
TJ is not exactly English ch, and SJ is not exactly English sh. Use the shortcut to predict, then use audio to learn the actual sound. Some loanwords are exceptions.

examples.fi: gäst · gissar · gillar
examples.en: soft G → Swedish j
examples.note: The first vowel is Ä or I.

examples.fi: Kina · köper · kött · tjej · tjuv
examples.en: soft K/TJ → /ɕ/
examples.note: Swedes call it the tjugo sound (tjugo = 20): a small, sharp hiss with the tongue forward. Do not add an English t + ch.

examples.fi: skärm · skiner · sjuk · skjorta
examples.en: SK/SJ/SKJ → sj sound /ɧ/
examples.note: The sju sound (sju = 7): deeper and further back than tj. It varies by region and speaker.

examples.fi: ska · skuld
examples.en: hard sk before A and U
examples.note: No front vowel follows sk.

examples.fi: Jag köper kött i Kina.
examples.en: I buy meat in China.
examples.note: One short sentence for repeated K + front-vowel practice.

rows: g + e, i, y, ä, ö
k + e, i, y, ä, ö
sk + e, i, y, ä, ö

sections.memoryTip: Same five soft vowels, three different results: G → J, K → TJ, SK → SJ. Tjugo (20) is the small, sharp sound; sju (7) is the big, deep one. Do not call them both ‘sh’.
sections.tryIt: Underline the first vowel in gillar, kött, and skärm. Predict the sound, listen, then repeat each word twice.

activity.label: Sound detective
activity.title: Look at the letter after g, k, or sk, then predict the sound
activity.instructions: Swedish teachers call e, i, y, ä, ö the soft vowels (mjuka vokaler) and a, o, u, å the hard vowels (hårda vokaler). Soft vowel next? The consonant usually softens too. Hard vowel next? It stays hard. Choose, then listen.

buckets.label: j sound
buckets.hint: as in ja · g + soft vowel

buckets.label: tj sound
buckets.hint: as in tjugo · k + soft vowel, or tj

buckets.label: sj sound
buckets.hint: as in sju · sk + soft vowel, sj, skj

buckets.label: No change
buckets.hint: a hard vowel (a, o, u, å) follows

items.why: G + ä, a front vowel: it starts like Swedish j.
K + i, a front vowel: the soft tj sound.
A is a back vowel, so sk stays hard: s + k.
Sk + ä, a front vowel: the sj sound.
G + i: the Swedish j sound.
A is a back vowel, so k stays hard.
K + ö: Ö is rounded but still a front vowel, so k softens.
Sj is always the sj sound, whatever vowel follows.
U is a back vowel, so sk stays hard.
K + ö, a front vowel: the tj sound.
Skj is always the sj sound, even before o.
G + i: the Swedish j sound.
Tj is always the tj sound.
Sk + i: the sj sound, as in Solen skiner.

activity.summary: One question does most of the work: which vowel comes next? Front vowels (e, i, y, ä, ö) soften g, k and sk into three different sounds; back vowels leave them hard. Sj, skj and tj keep their sound whatever follows. Some loanwords break the rule, so trust the recording.

sections.title: Recognise the remaining Lesson 1 spellings
body: Recognition only today: SJ and SKJ normally use the sj sound, as in sjuk and skjorta. Initial HJ and LJ normally begin with the Swedish j sound, as in hjälp and ljus.
Dialect matters in Finland: Sweden-Swedish often merges RS in kurs into a retroflex sound, while Finland-Swedish usually keeps R + S. Many Finland-Swedish speakers also keep a clear D in djur.
Och is /ɔk/ in careful speech and is often shorter in conversation. Skönt normally means pleasant or comfortable; say fint hår or snyggt hår for a natural compliment.

examples.fi: sjuk · skjorta
examples.en: sick · shirt
examples.note: Two spellings for the sj sound.

examples.fi: hjälp · ljus
examples.en: help · light
examples.note: Initial H or L is silent in these spellings; begin with Swedish j.

examples.fi: djur
examples.en: animal
examples.note: You may hear j alone in Sweden or a retained d in Finland-Swedish.

examples.fi: kurs · mars
examples.en: course · March/Mars
examples.note: Keep r + s separate for a Finland-Swedish target.

examples.fi: Jag gillar din rosa skjorta. Du har fint hår.
examples.en: I like your pink shirt. You have nice hair.
examples.note: The textbook uses skönt hår; fint hår is the natural compliment to produce.

sections.memoryTip: These are recognition words, not a second test. Your target is to notice the spelling and accept dialect variation.
sections.tryIt: Listen once to sjuk, skjorta, hjälp, ljus, djur, kurs, and mars. Copy the Finland-Swedish model you want to use; do not force every word into one accent.

assignment.title: Episode 1 mission: Say who you are
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Say your real four-line introduction once slowly and once at normal speed: name, home now, origin, and languages.

ONE SOUND LOOP: Choose only one: tak/tack OR gillar/kött/skärm. Listen and repeat the small set three times.

RETURN: Close the model and give your real introduction from memory in under 20 seconds.
assignment.model:
Hej! Jag heter Alex.
Jag bor i Helsingfors.
Jag kommer från Indien.
Jag talar hindi, engelska och lite svenska.

takeaways: Core: say Jag heter … · Jag bor i … · Jag kommer från … · Jag talar … as four complete chunks.
Mouth first, audio second: use the Hindi/Marathi/English bridge to find the shape, then copy the Swedish model.
Practise one contrast at a time: tak/tack or the g → j, k → tj, sk → sj pattern.

sections.title: Greet: choose the right question
body: In Finland, Hej is the everyday greeting everywhere: in shops, at work, and with friends. Finland-Swedish speakers often say Hej hej, and in southern Finland you will also hear the informal Morjens.
The everyday check-in is Hur är det? or Hur är det med dig? (How are things with you?). Very casual friends say Läget? or Hur är läget? (What's up?).
Hur mår du? asks more personally how someone feels. Friends use it too, and it is the natural question when someone has been ill or tired: Mår du bättre nu?

examples.fi: Hej! Hur är det med dig?
examples.en: Hi! How are things with you?
examples.note: A safe everyday check-in with anyone.

examples.fi: Hej hej! Hur är det?
examples.en: Hi! How's it going?
examples.note: Hej hej is very common in Finland-Swedish, as a greeting and as goodbye.

examples.fi: Morjens! Läget?
examples.en: Hey! What's up?
examples.note: Very casual. Recognise it; use it with friends.

examples.fi: Hur mår du? Mår du bättre nu?
examples.en: How are you feeling? Are you feeling better now?
examples.note: A real question about how someone feels.

sections.title: How are you? Pick an honest answer
body: Whichever question you hear, a short answer is enough: Bra, tack. Och du? You do not need to tell your whole day to someone you barely know.
Answer with the verb you hear: Hur är det? → Det är bra. Hur mår du? → Jag mår bra. You will also hear Jag är bra in casual speech, and Bara bra (just fine).
Then send the question back with Och du?, the same move you learned in Lesson 1.

examples.en: How's it going? — It's good, thanks.
examples.note: är det → det är: the answer mirrors the question.

examples.fi: Bara bra, tack! Och du?
examples.en: Just fine, thanks! And you?
examples.note: Bara bra is a very common short answer.

examples.fi: Jättebra!
examples.en: Really good!
examples.note: Jätte- makes it stronger. It works in any situation.

examples.fi: Hur mår du? — Jag mår toppen!
examples.en: How are you? — I feel great!
examples.note: Toppen means great, top.

examples.note: Lite from Lesson 1 makes it softer.

examples.fi: Jag mår ganska dåligt.
examples.en: I feel pretty bad.
examples.note: Ganska means pretty, rather.

examples.fi: Jag mår inte så bra.

activity.label: Mood meter
activity.title: Where does each answer sit on the mood meter?
activity.instructions: Read or hear each answer and place it on the meter. There is no wrong mood, only the right words for it.

items.why: Toppen is the top of the meter.
Bra means good or fine.
The answer to Hur är det? Same mood as Jag mår bra.
Bara bra: just fine. A very common short answer.
Så där is the middle: not good, not bad.
Okej is okay, the middle of the meter.
Jätte- makes bra stronger: really good.
Trött means tired: lower on the meter.
Dåligt means bad.
Jag mår + toppen: great.
Inte så bra: not so good.
Ganska dåligt: pretty bad.

activity.summary: Pick the answer that is true, then ask back with Och du? Honest answers make better conversations than always saying bra.

sections.title: Pronouns: point to people without names
body: Swedish subject pronouns: jag (I), du (you, one person), han (he), hon (she), hen (they, one person), vi (we), ni (you, two or more), de (they).
Count the people for you: du is singular (one person), ni is plural (two or more). Modern Swedish uses du with almost everyone, including teachers and shop staff.

Hen means one person without saying he or she. Use it when you do not know or it does not matter (En ny elev kommer. Hen heter Kim.), and for people who are neither he nor she. It works like Finnish hän. De is written de but said dom.
A common trap: someone and I together is vi (we). Anna och jag bor i Esbo. Vi talar svenska. When you talk to two people, use ni: Hej Sara och Peter! Talar ni svenska?

sections.title: People in your life: family and relationships
body: Family words are nouns: syster, bror, barn. Build sentences with the verbs har (have) and är (am): Jag har en syster. Jag är gift.

Swedish glues words together into compound words: pojke + vän = pojkvän (boyfriend), flicka + vän = flickvän (girlfriend). Bo means live, as in Jag bor i: a sambo lives together with a partner, a särbo lives apart.

Useful status words: gift (married), sambo, singel, skild (divorced; skilja sig = to get divorced), and Jag bor ensam (I live alone). Barn means child or children; syskon means brothers and sisters together.

examples.fi: Jag har en syster och en bror.
examples.en: I have a sister and a brother.
examples.note: En before one person: en syster, en bror.

examples.fi: Jag är sambo. Han heter Mikko.
examples.en: I live with my partner. His name is Mikko.
examples.note: Sambo: partners who live together without being married. Very common in Finland and Sweden.

examples.fi: Jag är gift. Jag har en fru.
examples.en: I'm married. I have a wife.
examples.note: Man = husband, fru = wife. Make and maka are formal words for spouse.

examples.fi: Jag är singel och jag bor ensam.
examples.en: I'm single and I live alone.
examples.note: Ensam = alone.

examples.fi: De har två barn, en son och en dotter.
examples.en: They have two children, a son and a daughter.
examples.note: Barn is both child and children.

rows: Jag är gift. Jag har en man.

sections.memoryTip: Bo = live. Jag bor i … (Lesson 1) → sambo (live together) → särbo (live apart). And a classic joke: gift means married, but ett gift is poison.

sections.title: Question words: ask the next question
body: Vad = what, hur = how, var = where, varifrån = where from, när = when, varför = why, vem = who.
Word order: question word → verb → subject (the person). Var bor du? När kommer de? The verb always comes second.
A yes/no question starts with the verb itself: Är du gift? Har du syskon? Talar du svenska? Vilken, vilket and vilka (which) come in a later lesson.

examples.en: What are you buying?
examples.note: Vad asks for a thing.

examples.fi: Hur är vädret?
examples.en: How is the weather?
examples.note: Hur asks how something is.

examples.fi: Hur gammal är du?
examples.en: How old are you?
examples.note: Hur + a describing word: hur gammal.

examples.fi: Var är Anna?
examples.en: Where is Anna?
examples.note: Var asks for a place.

examples.fi: När äter vi lunch?
examples.en: When do we eat lunch?
examples.note: När asks for a time.

examples.fi: Varför springer han?
examples.en: Why is he running?
examples.note: Varför asks for a reason.

examples.fi: Vem gillar du?
examples.en: Who do you like?
examples.note: Vem asks for a person.

sections.memoryTip: Var and vad differ by one letter: var asks for a place, vad for a thing. Varför hides för: for what reason?

sections.title: Hear it the way people say it
body: Written and spoken Swedish differ a little. Recognise these short forms now, and keep writing the full forms.
De is said dom. Jag is often just ja. Är often shrinks to e, det to de, and vad to va.
So Hur är det? often sounds like hur e de?, and De mår bra sounds like dom mår bra.

examples.fi: Vad heter du?

hunt.label: Help-verb and inte hunt

spots.rule: Inte (not) comes straight after the first verb: kan inte, vill inte, vet inte. In the command Oroa dig inte, it comes after oroa dig.
Kan (can) is a help verb. The next verb is an infinitive: kan läsa, kan sova. Kan du …? asks for help politely.
Vill (want to) is a help verb: vill sova.
Måste (must, have to) is a help verb: måste klara, måste sova, måste jobba.
Ska is a help verb too: vad jag ska göra = what I should do.

sections.title: Three verb forms: now, command, dictionary
body: A verb is a doing word. Today you need three verb forms. The present tense says what happens now or regularly. It ends in r: talar, köper, bor. The help verbs kan, vill, ska and måste are the exceptions, and so is vet (know) on page 8: Jag vet inte. Swedish uses the same form for I study and I am studying: Jag pluggar. Never say Jag är pluggar.

The imperative (command form) tells someone to do something: Tala! Köp! Ring! Your teacher calls it the naked verb. Later tenses are built on it, so it is worth learning well. The infinitive is the dictionary form. It follows a help verb and usually ends in a: tala, köpa, ringa. Dictionaries often show it with att (to): att tala = to speak.

Make the forms from the present tense, in three groups. Ar verbs: take away r. Talar becomes Tala! and tala; the command and the infinitive look the same. Er verbs: take away er for the command, then add a for the infinitive. Köper becomes Köp! and köpa. Short verbs: take away r. Bor becomes Bo! and bo; this infinitive does not end in a (also må).
Two verbs need extra care. Vara (be) is irregular: är in the present and Var! as a command. Kommer keeps only one m in the command: Kom! The infinitive is komma.

examples.fi: Jag talar svenska. · Tala svenska! · Jag kan tala svenska.
examples.en: I speak Swedish. · Speak Swedish! · I can speak Swedish.

examples.en: I buy bread. · Buy bread! · I want to buy bread.

examples.fi: Jag mår bra. · Må bra! · Jag vill må bättre.
examples.en: I feel well. · Be well! · I want to feel better.
examples.note: Short verb: mår loses r. The infinitive må does not end in a.

examples.fi: Han kommer hem. · Kom hem! · Han måste komma hem.
examples.en: He is coming home. · Come home! · He has to come home.
examples.note: Kommer keeps only one m in the command: Kom!

examples.en: I am happy. · Be happy! · I want to be happy.
examples.note: Vara is irregular: är in the present, Var! as a command.

items.why: Talar ends in r: it says what she does.
No r and no help verb: it tells someone to act.
It follows the help verb kan, so it is the infinitive.
Köper ends in r: present tense.
Köper loses er: Köp! is the command.
After vill, the verb ends in a: köpa.
Ringer loses er: Ring! is the command.
After måste, use the infinitive ringa.

sections.title: Help verbs open the door to an infinitive
body: Kan (can), vill (want to), måste (must, have to) and ska (will, be going to) are help verbs. The verb after them is always the infinitive: kan tala, vill köpa, måste jobba, ska träna. Never use the present tense there: kan tala, not kan talar.
Hinner (have time to) and orkar (have the energy to) work the same way: Jag hinner gå till affären. Jag orkar inte plugga.
Two useful questions. Kan du …? asks for help politely: Kan du hjälpa mig? Ska vi …? suggests a plan: Ska vi dricka kaffe? To want a thing, say vill ha: Jag vill ha kaffe, not Jag vill kaffe.

Careful: English must not is not måste inte in Swedish. A ban is får inte: Du får inte röka här (You must not smoke here). No need is behöver inte: Du behöver inte komma (You don’t have to come). Lecture 13 practises both.

sections.title: Inte comes after the first verb
body: Inte means not. It makes a sentence negative. Put inte straight after the first verb. One verb: Jag simmar inte. With a help verb: Jag kan inte simma. Kan is the first verb, so inte comes before the infinitive simma.

English adds do: I do not swim. Swedish never adds an extra verb. The rule works with every help verb: Jag vill inte ha kaffe. Jag hinner inte komma. In a command, inte also follows the verb: Läs inte mer! Oroa dig inte!

If you think in Hindi, watch out. Hindi puts nahīn before the verb (main nahīn jātā = I don’t go), so Jag inte går may feel right. Swedish wants Jag går inte. Marathi puts nāhī after the verb (mī jāt nāhī), which is closer to Swedish.
Short adverbs such as ofta (often), alltid (always) and aldrig (never) go in the same place as inte: Jag dricker ofta kaffe. Jag dricker aldrig vin.
Finland-Swedish note: in fast speech in Helsinki you will often hear int instead of inte. Recognise it, but write inte.

sections.title: The verb stays second
body: The golden rule of Swedish word order is verb second (V2): in a statement, the first verb is always the second building block. Position one can be the person (Min mamma bakar en kaka i dag), a time (I dag bakar min mamma en kaka) or a place (I Finland dricker vi mycket kaffe).

The subject always stands right next to the verb: just before it or just after it. When a time or a place comes first, the subject moves to just after the verb. Count chunks, not words: I dag is one chunk in position one.

With a help verb and inte: I morgon ska jag inte jobba. Ska is in position two, then jag, then inte, then the infinitive (verb 2) in its own slot. Questions with a question word follow the same rule: Varför kommer du sent?

Two common slips. English says Today I work, so learners say I dag jag jobbar. Swedish needs I dag jobbar jag. Hindi and Marathi put the verb near the end, so check that the verb has not drifted to the end. Learners of Swedish often master this swap late, so say time-first lines aloud many times.

assignment.title: Episode 3 mission: My week
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Say three things you can do, one thing you want to do, one thing you must do, and one thing you do not do this week.

CHANGE: Start two lines with I dag or I morgon and keep the verb second.

RETURN: Tomorrow, say a kan line, a måste line and a negative line without looking.

takeaways: Present tense usually ends in r; the command is the naked verb; the infinitive is the dictionary form that follows a help verb.
After kan, vill, måste and ska, use the infinitive: Jag kan tala.
Put inte after the first verb: Jag kan inte komma. In a command too: Oroa dig inte!
A time phrase may come first, but the verb stays second: I dag bakar min mamma en kaka.

sections.title: En or ett: every thing has a partner
body: Every Swedish noun belongs to one of two groups: en words and ett words. This is called noun gender. En and ett are articles: both mean a or an. En dator is a computer; ett jobb is a job. The group matters later too: it decides the word for “the” and the ending of describing words (Lecture 5).

The word itself rarely shows its group, so learn the article together with the noun. Most nouns, roughly 75–80%, are en words, so en is the better guess when you are not sure. Words for people are usually en words: en kvinna, en läkare. A useful exception is ett barn (a child).

Some endings give a clue. Nouns that end in -a are nearly always en words: en lista, en vecka (exceptions: ett öga, an eye; ett hjärta, a heart). Nouns that end in -are, -ing or -het are en words too: en lärare, en tidning (a newspaper), en frihet (freedom). Nouns that end in -um are ett words: ett museum, ett gymnasium.

A compound word is two words joined into one. The last part decides the gender. Dator is an en word, but spel is an ett word, so datorspel is an ett word: ett datorspel. Lista is an en word, so önskelista is too: en önskelista.

Hindi and Marathi also give every noun a gender, so the idea is not new to you. But en and ett are not male and female: en pojke (a boy) and en flicka (a girl) are both en words. Do not carry a gender over from Hindi or Marathi; learn the Swedish article.

sections.title: Work: what you do and where
body: Ask Vad jobbar du med? (What do you do for work?). The question ends in med, but the answer usually uses jobbar som plus the job: Jag jobbar som lärare. Do not put en or ett before the job. The same is true after är: Jag är lärare. English needs a; Swedish does not.

Use jobbar på plus the workplace. The workplace keeps its article: på en skola, på ett sjukhus, på ett kontor i stan (in town). A company name needs no article: på Ikea. Arbetar means the same as jobbar; it is a little more formal.

Hemifrån (from home) and mestadels (mostly) are adverbs: they say where from and how much. På distans means remotely. To name your field, use inom: Jag jobbar inom IT. Not working at the moment? Say Jag studerar or Jag söker jobb (I am looking for a job).

sections.title: Free time: what do you do?
body: The teacher’s homework question is Vad gör du på fritiden? (What do you do in your free time?). Answer with a verb in the present tense: Jag läser en bok. Jag lyssnar på musik. Jag tränar på gymmet.

English uses play for everything. Swedish has two verbs. Spelar is for games, sports and instruments: spelar datorspel, spelar fotboll, spelar piano. Leker is free play, the way children and pets play: leker med min katt.

Some free time is at home: stannar hemma (stay at home), vilar (rest), lagar mat (cook). Some is away: åker till havet (go to the sea), åker skidor (ski), reser utomlands (travel abroad), går på bio (go to the cinema). Går en kurs means takes a course: en språkkurs, en matlagningskurs.

Semester is a holiday from work (not a school term): Jag har semester or Jag är på semester. Fikar means having coffee and something sweet. Swedes say it all the time; in Finland, Swedish speakers usually say dricker kaffe.

sections.title: Habits: brukar and time phrases
body: Brukar means usually: it says that something is a habit, something you do regularly. Brukar is itself a verb in the present tense. The action after it stays in the infinitive (the basic form), with no att: brukar läsa, not brukar att läsa. Careful: brukar is not English used to, which is about the past. Jag brukar läsa means I usually read, now.

A time phrase can come first. Then the verb comes second and the subject comes after it: På helgen brukar jag läsa. This is the same word order as I dag ska jag träna in Lecture 3. For a negative, put inte right after brukar and the subject: Jag brukar inte träna. På helgen brukar jag inte träna.

Useful time phrases: på fritiden (in your free time), på helgen (at the weekend), på morgonen (in the morning), på eftermiddagen (in the afternoon), på kvällen (in the evening) and då och då (now and then, the same as ibland). Så fort som möjligt means as soon as possible.

Watch the small preposition before the time. På + kvällen, helgen, morgonen often describes a habit: på kvällen = in the evening, any evening. I + the time points to one particular time: i kväll = tonight, i helgen = this weekend. A trap: i morgon (Lecture 3) means tomorrow; in the morning is på morgonen. In Finland you will often hear på veckoslutet instead of på helgen; both are correct.

examples.en: At the weekend I usually read a book.
examples.note: Time first, then brukar, then jag.

examples.note: På kvällen = a habit; i kväll = this one evening.

assignment.title: Episode 4 mission: My work and free time
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Say five lines: what you do, where you do it, and details about your work arrangement and free time. Use brukar for at least one regular habit and a time phrase such as på helgen.

WRITE: Post your 25–45 word language-exchange profile. Check that som + profession has no article.

RETURN: Tomorrow, say your work or study line and two habits without looking.
assignment.model: Jag jobbar som programmerare. Jag jobbar på ett företag i Helsingfors, men jag jobbar mestadels hemifrån. På helgen brukar jag läsa en bok. På kvällen lyssnar jag på musik. Då och då går jag på bio.

takeaways: Learn a noun with its article: en dator, ett jobb. Most nouns are en words, and endings help (-a, -ing, -are: en; -um: ett). The last part decides a compound word: ett datorspel.
Work: jobbar som + profession without an article; jobbar på + workplace with its article.
Free time: spelar for games, sports and instruments; leker for free play with children and pets.
Habits: brukar + infinitive, with no att. Put a time first and keep the verb second: På helgen brukar jag läsa. På helgen = every weekend; i helgen = this weekend.

pages.title: Textbook page practice: Min dröm
pages.intro: Sara wants to follow her father into photography. Her father wants a new direction. Listen for two different dreams.

setting.fi: Sara är 15 år. Saras pappa, Peter, är 45 år.
setting.en: Sara is 15 (femton). Her father, Peter, is 45 (fyrtiofem).

pages.imageAlt: Textbook page Min dröm, with Sara and her father Peter describing their career dreams
recallCues: Sara says she wants to become a photographer when she grows up and explains her interests and role model.
Peter is tired of photography, wants to try journalism and is taking a course now.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.fi: Jag vill bli fotograf när jag blir stor. Jag är mycket intresserad av mode och smink så jag vill jobba på en modetidning som till exempel Vogue. Min pappa är fotograf. Jag ser upp till honom.
lines.en: I want to become a photographer when I grow up. I am very interested in fashion and make-up, so I want to work for a fashion magazine such as Vogue. My father is a photographer. I look up to him.

lines.speaker: Peter
lines.fi: Jag är trött på att jobba som fotograf. Nu vill jag prova att vara journalist. Det är inte lätt att byta jobb men jag ska riskera. Just nu går jag en kurs i journalistik. Där läser jag och skriver mycket.
lines.en: I am tired of working as a photographer. Now I want to try being a journalist. It is not easy to change jobs, but I am going to take a risk. Right now I am taking a course in journalism. There I read and write a lot.

glossary.en: I am going to take the risk (see the note)

listenQuestions.prompt: What does Sara want to become?

listenQuestions.explanation: Just nu går jag en kurs i journalistik.

naturalNotes.note: The source is understandable. In everyday Swedish, ta risken or våga prova is more idiomatic for “take the risk”. Recognise the source, but use Jag ska ta risken.

chunks: Min pappa är fotograf. Jag ser upp till honom.

hunt.instructions: The page marks whole phrases in red or with a line. Tap the first word of each marked phrase and read what it does.
hunt.missHint: Tap the first word of a red or underlined phrase.

spots.rule: Intresserad av means interested in. The small word is always av.
Så introduces the result: Sara is interested in fashion, so she wants a fashion-magazine job.
Till exempel means for example. Till also ends the phrase ser upp till.
Ser upp till means look up to, admire.
Trött på says you have had enough of something: tired of.
Prova means try. Prova att vara: try being.
Lätt means easy. Det är inte lätt: it is not easy.
Byta jobb means change jobs. The present tense is byter.
Går en kurs means takes or attends a course.

pages.title: Textbook page practice: En rolig film, ett roligt jobb
pages.tabLabel: Page 15 · En rolig film, ett roligt jobb
pages.intro: Maria and Nora use en and ett descriptions while talking about homes, jobs and a film. Watch the -t ending.
pages.imageAlt: Textbook page En rolig film, ett roligt jobb, where Maria and Nora discuss homes, work and a film
focus: bestämd form av substantiv: kafeet, livet, jobbet
recallCues: The narrator describes their small town, the small full café, what they talk about and Maria’s fun plan.
Maria says she and Peter want a new home, but disagree between a city flat and a country house.
Nora hopes they agree, then says she needs a fun new job because her boss is strict.
Maria invites Nora to the cinema because a fun film makes her feel better.

lines.speaker: Berättare
lines.fi: Maria och Nora bor i en liten stad och träffas på ett litet kafe. Kafeet är fullt. De pratar om livet och helgen. Maria har en rolig plan.
lines.en: Maria and Nora live in a small town and meet at a small café. The café is full. They talk about life and the weekend. Maria has a fun plan.

glossary.en: full (ett form, because kafe is an ett-word)

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.fi: Peter och jag letar efter ett nytt hem. Peter vill gärna köpa en ny lägenhet i stan men jag tycker att ett charmigt hus på landet är bättre.
lines.en: Peter and I are looking for a new home. Peter would like to buy a new flat in town, but I think a charming house in the countryside is better.

lines.speaker: Nora
lines.fi: Jag hoppas att ni kan komma överens. Jag har ett stort problem på jobbet. Chefen är så sträng. Jag måste hitta ett roligt nytt jobb.
lines.en: I hope you can agree. I have a big problem at work. The boss is so strict. I must find a fun new job.

glossary.en: I hope (not hoppar, which means jump)
the boss (a chef in Swedish is a boss, not a cook)

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.fi: Jag förstår. Du är kanske stressad. Vill du gå på bio med mig ikväll? Du mår alltid bättre efter en rolig film.
lines.en: I understand. Perhaps you are stressed. Do you want to go to the cinema with me tonight? You always feel better after a fun film.

naturalNotes.source: ett litet kafe. Kafeet är fullt.

naturalNotes.note: The page leaves out the accent. Write kafé and kaféet in your own Swedish; the sound is the same.
Stan is the everyday short form of staden (the town). Both are correct; stan is what you hear most.

hunt.label: Ending hunt
hunt.title: Find the forms marked on the page
hunt.instructions: Tap each red or underlined word. Decide: an adjective for an en-word, an adjective for an ett-word, or a noun meaning “the”.
hunt.missHint: Look for the red describing words and the underlined nouns.

spots.rule: En liten stad: stad is an en-word, so liten keeps its basic form.
Ett litet kafe: liten becomes litet with an ett-word.
Kafeet means the café: ett kafe takes -et. Dictionary spelling: kaféet.
Kafeet är fullt: kafe is an ett-word, so full takes -t, even after är.
Livet means life: ett liv takes -et. Swedish uses the definite form for life in general.
Helgen means the weekend: en helg takes -en.
En rolig plan, en rolig film: en-words, so rolig has no -t.
Ett nytt hem, ett roligt nytt jobb: ny becomes nytt with an ett-word.
En ny lägenhet: lägenhet is an en-word, so ny has no -t.
Ett charmigt hus: charmig adds -t for an ett-word.
Landet: ett land takes -et. På landet means in the countryside.
Ett stort problem: stor adds -t for an ett-word.
Jobbet means the job: ett jobb takes -et. På jobbet means at work.
Chefen means the boss: en chef takes -en.
Chefen är sträng: chef is an en-word, so sträng has no -t.
Ett roligt nytt jobb: rolig adds -t because jobb is an ett-word.

She wants to stop studying Swedish.
She wants to buy a café.

sections.title: Say what you dream about
body: A dream can be a job, a home or something you want to learn. Use Jag drömmer om + a thing: Jag drömmer om ett hus. Use Jag vill bli + a job when you mean “I want to become”. After bli, a job has no en or ett: Jag vill bli fotograf.

Blir is the present tense of bli: När jag blir stor means when I grow up. Some words always bring the same small word with them, so learn them as chunks: intresserad av (interested in), ser upp till (look up to), trött på (tired of). English “interested in” tempts you to say intresserad i. Swedish always says intresserad av.
Byta jobb means change jobs; byta kläder means change clothes. The present tense is byter: Jag byter jobb. Går en kurs means takes or attends a course.

examples.fi: Jag drömmer om ett roligt jobb.
examples.en: I dream about a fun job.

examples.fi: Maja vill bli fotograf.
examples.en: Maja wants to become a photographer.

examples.fi: Alex är intresserad av fotografering.
examples.en: Alex is interested in photography.

examples.fi: Jag ser upp till min mamma.
examples.en: I look up to my mother.

examples.fi: Först går jag en kurs, och sedan byter jag jobb.
examples.en: First I take a course, and then I change jobs.

sections.memoryTip: Drömmer om points to the dream. Vill bli points to the person or job you want to become.
sections.tryIt: Finish aloud: Jag drömmer om … Jag är intresserad av … Jag vill …

activity.label: Dream builder
activity.title: Give each phrase its small word
activity.instructions: Each start needs its own small word: om, av, till or på. Match the pairs, then say each complete sentence.
activity.pattern: Learn the small word with the phrase: drömmer om, intresserad av, ser upp till, trött på. After bli, the job has no en or ett.

sections.title: Link one idea to the next
body: A conjunction is a small linking word. Och adds. Eller gives a choice. Men makes a contrast. Så gives a result. För gives a reason: here it means because.
After och, men, så and för, keep the normal order: the person, then the verb (så jag är trött). In writing, put a comma before men, så and för when a whole sentence follows.

Put the för part after the main idea: Jag kan inte träna, för jag är trött. English often starts with “Because …”, but Swedish för cannot start a sentence that way. Another word, eftersom, does that job later in the course.

Sedan (then) is a time adverb, not a conjunction. When it starts a sentence, the verb comes second, so the verb goes before the person: Sedan åker jag till jobbet. In speech, sedan is often shortened to sen. That is a spoken form.

examples.fi: Jag är intresserad av mode och smink.
examples.en: I am interested in fashion and make-up.

examples.fi: Vi kan dricka kaffe eller te.
examples.en: We can drink coffee or tea.

examples.fi: Jag vill träna, men jag hinner inte i dag.
examples.en: I want to exercise, but I do not have time today.

examples.fi: Jag pluggar svenska, så jag kan klara YKI-testet.
examples.en: I study Swedish, so I can pass the YKI test.

examples.fi: Jag kan inte sova, för jag dricker mycket kaffe.
examples.en: I cannot sleep because I drink a lot of coffee.

examples.fi: Jag äter frukost, och sedan åker jag till jobbet.
examples.en: I eat breakfast, and then I go to work.

sections.memoryTip: Reason → så → result. Result → för → reason. Your other languages help: för is like Hindi kyunki and Marathi karan (because); så is like Hindi isliye and Marathi mhanun (so).
sections.tryIt: Join aloud with men: Jag är trött. Jag vill prova. → Jag är trött, men jag vill prova.

activity.label: Join the ideas
activity.title: Which link makes sense?
activity.instructions: The linking word is missing. Read both ideas and choose the link that makes sense. Then say the whole sentence aloud with the link and a comma.

items.fi: Jag jobbar mycket … jag är trött.
items.en: I work a lot … I am tired.
items.why: Tired is the result of a lot of work: Jag jobbar mycket, så jag är trött.

items.fi: Jag är trött … jag jobbar mycket.
items.en: I am tired … I work a lot.
items.why: Now the reason comes second: Jag är trött, för jag jobbar mycket.

items.fi: Jag vill träna … jag hinner inte i dag.
items.en: I want to exercise … I do not have time today.
items.why: The second idea turns against the first: Jag vill träna, men jag hinner inte i dag.
You choose one of two: kaffe eller te.

items.fi: Jag pluggar svenska … jag vill klara YKI-testet.
items.en: I study Swedish … I want to pass the YKI test.
items.why: Passing YKI is the reason you study: Jag pluggar svenska, för jag vill klara YKI-testet.

items.fi: Jag har ett prov snart … jag pluggar mycket.
items.en: I have a test soon … I study a lot.
items.why: Studying a lot is the result of the test: Jag har ett prov snart, så jag pluggar mycket.

items.fi: Jag gillar kaffe … te är bättre.
items.en: I like coffee … tea is better.
items.why: A contrast: Jag gillar kaffe, men te är bättre.

items.fi: Jag vill byta jobb … chefen är sträng.
items.en: I want to change jobs … the boss is strict.
items.why: The strict boss is the reason: Jag vill byta jobb, för chefen är sträng.

activity.summary: Ask: is the second idea the result (så) or the reason (för)? Swap the two ideas and så becomes för.

sections.title: Put “the” on the end
body: English puts the article “the” in front of a noun. Swedish usually adds it to the end of the noun instead. This is the definite form. An en-word adds -en or -n. An ett-word adds -et or -t. Hindi and Marathi have no words for “a” and “the”, so it is easy to leave them out. Check every noun: en or ett, or the ending?

Learn each noun as a pair: en bok → boken, ett hus → huset. A word that already ends in a vowel adds only -n or -t: kvinna → kvinnan, äpple → äpplet. A few words that end in -el or -er also add only -n: en cykel → cykeln, en vinter → vintern.

When do you use it? Use en or ett the first time you mention something. Use the definite form when you both know which one you mean: Jag har en bil. Bilen är tysk. Some words are almost always definite: på jobbet (at work), i skolan (at school), livet (life) and världen (the world).

examples.fi: Jag har en bil. Bilen är tysk.
examples.en: I have a car. The car is German.

examples.fi: Jag har en snäll kollega på jobbet. Kollegan kommer från Sverige.
examples.en: I have a kind colleague at work. The colleague comes from Sweden.

examples.fi: På jobbet arbetar jag mycket.
examples.en: At work I work a lot.

examples.fi: I skolan läser vi svenska varje dag.
examples.en: At school we study Swedish every day.

examples.fi: Vi pratar om livet och världen.
examples.en: We talk about life and the world.

sections.memoryTip: The small word en or ett moves to the back: en bok → bok-en; ett hus → hus-et.
sections.tryIt: Point to one familiar thing and say both forms: en bok, boken.

activity.label: Ending sort
activity.title: Predict the ending for “the”
activity.instructions: Each card shows a noun with en or ett. Say the “the” form aloud first, then choose the ending you added.

items.why: En-word that ends in a consonant: en bok → boken.
Ett-word that ends in a consonant: ett hus → huset.
En-word that already ends in a vowel: en kamera → kameran.
Ett-word that already ends in a vowel: ett äpple → äpplet.
ett jobb → jobbet, as in på jobbet.
Ends in a vowel: en skola → skolan, as in i skolan.
en värld → världen.
An exception to the vowel clue: kafé ends in a stressed é, so it adds -et: kaféet, as on page 15.

activity.summary: En-word → -en or -n. Ett-word → -et or -t. Ending in a vowel → just -n or -t (but kaféet). Learn every noun with en or ett.

sections.title: Make the describing word fit
body: An adjective describes a noun: a fun film, a fun job. In Swedish the adjective changes to fit the noun’s group. This is called agreement. Use rolig with an en-word and roligt with an ett-word.

Most adjectives just add -t for an ett-word: rolig → roligt, stor → stort, gammal → gammalt, vacker → vackert. Two common ones change more: ny → nytt (double t) and liten → litet. Adjectives that already end in -t stay the same: ett lätt jobb, ett trött barn. A few never change, such as bra: en bra film, ett bra jobb.

The same ending comes after är: Boken är rolig. Huset är stort. Kaféet är fullt. After det är, use the -t form too: Det är roligt! Det är inte lätt. These forms are for one thing (singular); plural forms come later.
Lite (a little) is a different word. It is an adverb: it tells how much, and it never changes. Jag pratar lite svenska. Never say liten svenska.

examples.fi: Jag läser en rolig bok.
examples.en: I am reading a fun book.

examples.fi: Jag har ett roligt jobb.
examples.en: I have a fun job.

examples.fi: Vi bor i ett litet hus.
examples.en: We live in a small house.

examples.fi: Huset är stort.
examples.en: The house is big.

examples.fi: Det är inte lätt, men det är roligt.
examples.en: It is not easy, but it is fun.

examples.fi: Jag pratar lite svenska.
examples.en: I speak a little Swedish.

sections.memoryTip: Hear ett, expect a -t sound on the adjective too: ett roligt jobb.
sections.tryIt: Say the pairs aloud: rolig film, roligt jobb; stor lägenhet, stort hus; liten paus, litet barn.

activity.label: En or ett?
activity.title: Read the adjective, find the noun’s group
activity.instructions: The small word en or ett is hidden. Look at the adjective’s ending and decide which group the noun belongs to. Then say the phrase with en or ett.

buckets.label: en-word
buckets.hint: The adjective has its basic form: rolig, liten, gammal.

buckets.label: ett-word
buckets.hint: The adjective has its -t form: roligt, nytt, litet.

items.why: No -t on rolig, so bok is an en-word: en rolig bok.
Roligt has -t, so jobb is an ett-word: ett roligt jobb.
Tråkigt has -t: ett tråkigt möte.
No -t on farlig: en farlig hund.
Ny becomes nytt with an ett-word: ett nytt kafé.
Liten is the en form: en liten paus.
Liten becomes litet with an ett-word: ett litet barn.
No -t on gammal: en gammal vän.

activity.summary: The noun’s group controls the adjective. Learn en or ett with every new noun.

guided.hint: Use the amount word lite, not the adjective liten. Pratar, talar or kan all work.

guided.prompt: Build the next step: “First I take a course, and then I apply for a job.”
answers: Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag jobb.
Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag ett jobb.
Först går jag en kurs, och sen söker jag jobb.
Först går jag en kurs, och sen söker jag ett jobb.

checkpoint.prompt: Write in Swedish: “The job is boring, so I want a new job.”
answers: Jobbet är tråkigt, så jag vill ha ett nytt jobb.
Jobbet är tråkigt, så jag vill ha ett nytt arbete.
Arbetet är tråkigt, så jag vill ha ett nytt arbete.
Arbetet är tråkigt, så jag vill ha ett nytt jobb.
checkpoint.hint: Start with “the job” (definite form). Jobb is an ett-word, so both adjectives take -t. Link with så.
checkpoint.explanation: Jobbet är tråkigt, så jag vill ha ett nytt jobb: jobbet means the job, tråkigt and nytt fit the ett-word jobb, and så gives the result.

checkpoint.prompt: Which pair means “a house → the house”?
checkpoint.explanation: Ett hus takes the definite ending -et.

checkpoint.prompt: Which phrase is correct?
checkpoint.explanation: Ett kafé needs litet.

checkpoint.prompt: Which line gives a reason, not a result?
answers: Jag går en kurs, för jag vill byta jobb.
options: Jag går en kurs, för jag vill byta jobb.
Jag vill byta jobb, så jag går en kurs.
Jag går en kurs, och sedan söker jag jobb.

checkpoint.prompt: Write in Swedish: “I have a camera. The camera is old.”
answers: Jag har en kamera. Kameran är gammal.
checkpoint.hint: First mention: en kamera. Second mention: the definite form. Kamera ends in a vowel.
checkpoint.explanation: Jag har en kamera. Kameran är gammal: the second time, both people know which camera, so it becomes kameran.

assignment.title: Episode 5 mission: My dream
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Tell Elin your dream in five or six linked sentences. Say what you dream about, what interests you, what you want to do, why, one difficulty, and one next step. Use men, så and för.

WRITING: Reply to your friend’s question Vad drömmer du om? Include the dream, the reason and one thing you will try.

RETURN: Tomorrow, say your dream and reason from memory in under 30 seconds.
assignment.model: Jag drömmer om ett roligt jobb. Jag är intresserad av språk och fotografering, så jag vill göra något kreativt. Jag vill byta jobb, för jag vill lära mig något nytt. Det är inte lätt, men jag vill prova. Först går jag en kurs, och sedan söker jag ett nytt jobb.

takeaways: Link ideas: och adds, eller offers a choice, men contrasts, så gives a result, för gives a reason, and sedan moves to the next action.
Put “the” on the noun: en bok → boken, ett hus → huset, en kvinna → kvinnan, ett äpple → äpplet.
Let the adjective follow en or ett: en rolig film but ett roligt jobb; ny → nytt and liten → litet; after det är: Det är roligt. Lite (a little) never changes.

dialogue.speaker: Elin
dialogue.fi: Hej Alex! Det här är Maja. Hon är sjutton år och går i gymnasiet.
dialogue.en: Hi Alex! This is Maja. She is seventeen and goes to upper secondary school.

dialogue.speaker: Maja

dialogue.speaker: Elin
dialogue.fi: Maja, vad drömmer du om?

dialogue.speaker: Maja
dialogue.fi: Jag drömmer om ett roligt jobb. Jag vill bli fotograf.
dialogue.en: I dream about a fun job. I want to become a photographer.

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.fi: Titta, en bild från Helsingfors! Jag har en gammal kamera.
dialogue.en: Look, a picture from Helsinki! I have an old camera.

dialogue.speaker: Maja
dialogue.fi: Kameran är gammal, men bilden är fin!

dialogue.speaker: Alex
dialogue.fi: Tack! Jag vill gå en kurs, för jag vill lära mig mer.

reading_passage.text:
Hej Elin!
Tack för i dag! Alex är trevlig. Jag vill bli fotograf, för jag är intresserad av natur och konst. Nästa år vill jag gå en kurs i fotografering. Kursen är dyr, så jag jobbar på ett litet kafé på lördagar. Jobbet är ibland tråkigt, men chefen är snäll och kaféet är charmigt. Just nu pluggar jag mycket, för jag har ett prov snart. Sedan har jag mer tid.
Kram,
Maja

sections.title: Build regular past forms
body: Past tense tells what happened at a finished time: igår (yesterday), igår kväll (yesterday evening), i lördags (last Saturday: i + day + s), förra veckan (last week), förra året (last year). For “ago”, put the time between för and sedan: för fem år sedan = five years ago. Sedan on its own means then: Sedan gick jag hem.
The past form is the same for every person: jag jobbade, du jobbade, hon jobbade, vi jobbade. Unlike Hindi (gaya, gayi, gaye) or English (was, were), it never changes for a man, a woman or a group.
Your teacher’s clue: look at the present tense form. Verbs with -ar in the present are group 1. Keep the -a of the base form and add -de: jobbar → jobba → jobbade, dansar → dansade.

Most group 2 verbs have -er in the present. Take away -er and add -de: ringer → ringde, beställer → beställde. If what is left ends in p, k, t, s or x, add -te instead: köper → köpte, tycker → tyckte, läser → läste. These sounds are voiceless: your throat does not buzz when you say them. The -te rule is only for -er verbs; pratar is group 1, so it becomes pratade.

Group 3 verbs are short and end in a vowel + r in the present: bor, mår, tror. They add -dde: bodde, mådde, trodde. Careful: some of the most common verbs break these patterns (har → hade, tar → tog, går → gick, äter → åt). Learn those as pairs in the next topic.
When a time word comes first, the verb still comes second and jag moves after it: Igår jobbade jag. Not: Igår jag jobbade. This is the verb-second word order from Lecture 3.

buckets.label: -te
buckets.hint: -er after p, k, t, s, x

items.why: Dansar ends in -ar: group 1. Dansar → dansade.
Pratar ends in -ar: group 1, even though the stem has a t. Pratar → pratade.
Lagar ends in -ar: group 1. Lagar → lagade.
Ringer ends in -er and ring ends in ng, a buzzing sound. Ringer → ringde.
Beställ ends in l, a buzzing sound. Beställer → beställde.
Köp ends in p, a voiceless sound. Köper → köpte.
Tyck ends in a k sound. Tycker → tyckte.
Läs ends in s. Läser → läste.
Bor is bo + r: a short verb ending in a vowel. Bor → bodde.
Mår is må + r: a short verb ending in a vowel. Mår → mådde.

activity.summary: Read the present form first: -ar → -ade; -er → -de, or -te after p, k, t, s, x; short verbs with a vowel + r → -dde. Very common verbs such as går, äter and har are irregular: learn them as pairs.

sections.title: Learn the common irregular pairs
body: Some very common verbs do not follow the regular patterns. Often the vowel inside the verb changes (dricker → drack, skriver → skrev); sometimes the whole word changes (är → var). Learn each present–past pair as one chunk. The textbook calls them starka verb (strong verbs); this course calls them irregular verbs.

Start with the forms you need to tell a whole day: är → var, har → hade, går → gick, äter → åt, dricker → drack, sover → sov, gör → gjorde, kommer → kom. Page 18 has ten more. Learn a few each day in your diary.
A trap: var can mean was (Jag var hemma) or where (Var bor du?), so Var var du? means Where were you?

Swedish has no did. In a yes/no question the past verb simply comes first: Åt du frukost? (Did you eat breakfast?) Hade du en bra dag på jobbet? (Did you have a good day at work?) In a negative sentence inte comes after the past verb: Jag sov inte bra. (I did not sleep well.) Never use gjorde for did: Åt du? (not Gjorde du äta?)

examples.en: I was at home all evening.

examples.fi: Vi åt middag och drack kaffe.
examples.en: We ate dinner and drank coffee.

examples.fi: Maja gick hem klockan åtta.
examples.en: Maja went home at eight.

examples.fi: Hade du en bra dag på jobbet?
examples.en: Did you have a good day at work?

sections.memoryTip: Learn them in sound families: går–gick and får–fick; skriver–skrev and blir–blev; vill–ville and kan–kunde. Gick and gjorde both start with a y sound.
sections.tryIt: Cover the past column and say all eight past forms. Then ask one question without did, for example Åt du frukost?, and answer it: Ja, jag åt … / Nej, jag åt inte …

activity.label: Irregular pairs
activity.title: Match the present to the past
activity.instructions: Match each present form to its past form, then say each pair aloud.

pairs.note: Igår var jag trött. (Yesterday I was tired.)
Vi hade fest. (We had a party.)
Vad gjorde du? (What did you do?)
Jag kom hem sent. (I came home late.)

activity.pattern: There is no single ending rule. Often the vowel changes (dricker → drack); sometimes the whole word changes (är → var). Learn them as pairs.

sections.title: React to good news
body: A story about the past is also a conversation. When a friend tells you news, react first, then ask one follow-up question.

Big good news: Vilka fantastiska nyheter! (What fantastic news!) or Grattis! (Congratulations!). Nyheter is plural in Swedish (en nyhet = one piece of news), so you say vilka, not vilken. Smaller good news: Vad roligt! (How nice!) or Vad bra! (How good!). Bad news: Vad tråkigt! (What a pity!). Tråkig also means boring, but as a reaction it means I am sorry to hear that. Surprise: Oj! (Oh!). Jag är stolt över dig means I am proud of you.
Then ask a past question: Hur var det? (How was it?) or Vad gjorde du? (What did you do?).

examples.fi: Vilka fantastiska nyheter! Grattis!
examples.en: What fantastic news! Congratulations!

examples.fi: Jag är så stolt över dig.
examples.en: I am so proud of you.

examples.fi: Vad roligt! Hur var det?
examples.en: How nice! How was it?

examples.fi: Hur var det på festen?
examples.en: How was the party?

examples.en: Oh, what a pity! How are you now?

sections.memoryTip: React + ask: Vad roligt! Hur var det?
sections.tryIt: Your friend says Jag klarade provet! React and ask one past question.

activity.label: News response
activity.title: Match each news line to a natural response
activity.instructions: Make four mini-conversations and say both parts.

pairs.right: Grattis! Jag är stolt över dig.
pairs.note: I passed the test! — Congratulations! I am proud of you.
We had a party yesterday. — How nice! How was it?

pairs.right: Vad bra! Vilken bok köpte du?
pairs.note: I bought a new book. — Good! Which book did you buy?

pairs.right: Oj, vad tråkigt! Hur mår du nu?
pairs.note: I was ill at the weekend. — Oh, what a pity! How are you now?

activity.pattern: Show that you listened before you ask for more.

sections.title: Go home, then be at home
body: Hem shows direction: you move toward home. Hemma shows location: you are already there. English says “home” for both, so look at the verb.

Movement verbs take hem: gå hem (go home on foot), åka hem (go home by bus, tram or car), komma hem. Being or doing something there takes hemma: Jag var hemma. Jag jobbade hemma. Hemma åt jag middag. Åker → åkte is regular: -te after k.
The same idea works for ut–ute (out–outside), in–inne (in–inside), upp–uppe (up–upstairs) and ner–nere (down–downstairs). The short form shows movement; the form ending in -a or -e shows location.
Two useful chunks: hem till mig (to my place) and hemma hos mig (at my place).

examples.fi: Det är sent. Jag måste gå hem.
examples.en: It is late. I have to go home.

examples.fi: Jag är hemma, kom när du vill!
examples.en: I am at home, come when you like!

examples.fi: Igår åkte jag hem klockan fem.
examples.en: Yesterday I went home at five.

examples.fi: Kom hem till mig på fredag!
examples.en: Come to my place on Friday!

examples.fi: Hissen går upp. Jag är uppe på andra våningen.
examples.en: The lift goes up. I am up on the second floor.

sections.memoryTip: Moving toward home (gå, åka, komma)? Say hem. Already at home (vara, jobba, äta)? Say hemma.
sections.tryIt: Say two linked lines: Igår gick jag hem … Hemma …

activity.label: Move or stay
activity.title: Movement or location: which word is missing?
activity.instructions: Look at the highlighted verb and the English. Does the missing word show movement (hem, ut, upp) or location (hemma, ute, uppe)? Choose, then say the full sentence aloud.

items.en: Yesterday I went home at six.
items.why: Gick is movement toward home: Igår gick jag hem klockan sex.

items.en: I was at home all evening.
items.why: Var tells where you were: Jag var hemma hela kvällen.
Åkte is movement: Jag åkte hem med bussen.
You worked in a place; you did not move there: Jag jobbade hemma igår.

items.en: Come to my place on Friday!
items.why: Komma is movement toward a home: Kom hem till mig på fredag!
Gå shows movement: Jag måste gå ut.

items.en: I am outside with the dog.
items.why: Är tells where you are: Jag är ute med hunden.
The lift moves: Hissen går upp.

items.en: I am up on the second floor.
items.why: You are already there: Jag är uppe på andra våningen.

activity.summary: Short form for direction (hem, ut, upp); the form ending in -a or -e for location (hemma, ute, uppe).

Hade du en bra dag på arbetet?

answers: Vi åt middag och drack kaffe.

listening.text: Igår sov Elin länge. Hon vaknade klockan elva och drack kaffe hemma. Sedan ringde hon en vän. På eftermiddagen gick hon ut och köpte mat. Hon gick en promenad i parken. Klockan fem gick hon hem och lagade soppa. På kvällen läste hon en bok. Hon var trött och sov bra.

reading_passage.text:
Majas dagbok, söndag
Idag fick jag veta att jag klarade matteprovet! Jag blev så glad. Jag pluggade mycket förra veckan. Mamma sa: ”Jag är så stolt över dig.” På eftermiddagen firade vi hemma. Vi åt tårta och drack kaffe. Sedan ringde jag en kompis och berättade allt. Nu är jag trött men glad. God natt!

writing.prompt: Write your first short diary entry about yesterday in five to seven sentences.
writing.situation: Your Swedish teacher asks you to keep a diary in Swedish: 5–10 minutes every day, in the past tense. Write your first entry, about yesterday.
points: Say when it happened (Igår …) and tell your morning.
Say where you went or where you were (use hem or hemma once).
Name one person in your life you met, called or talked to.
Use at least two irregular past forms, such as var, åt or gick.
End with your evening and what you liked or did not like about the day.
writing.help: Igår vaknade jag … · Sedan åkte/gick jag till … · Där pratade jag med … · Efter jobbet ringde jag … · Hemma åt jag … · Dagen var …, men jag gillade …
writing.model: Igår vaknade jag tidigt och drack kaffe. Sedan åkte jag till jobbet. Där pratade jag med min kollega. Efter jobbet ringde jag min mamma. Klockan sex gick jag hem. Hemma åt jag en god middag och pluggade svenska. Dagen var lång, men jag gillade kvällen.

route.expectedOutput: Tell Elin about yesterday in six past-tense lines, then write a 35–60-word diary entry.
route.transferPrompt: Change one detail: tell the same day with a different meal, place or evening activity.
route.returnPrompt: Tomorrow, retell yesterday from memory in under 40 seconds with four past verbs.
successChecks: Move from morning to evening in a clear order.
Use at least four correct past-tense verbs.
Include one regular and one irregular past form.
Use hem for movement or hemma for location correctly.

assignment.title: Episode 6 mission: Yesterday
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Tell Elin what you did yesterday in six lines, from morning to evening. Use at least four past verbs.

WRITING: Start your diary with five to seven sentences about yesterday.

DAILY: Continue the diary for 5–10 minutes every day, as your teacher asked. Each day, use at least two irregular past forms and one new word about your own life.

RETURN: Tomorrow, retell the day without looking.
assignment.model: Igår vaknade jag klockan sju och åt frukost. Sedan åkte jag till jobbet med bussen. På jobbet pratade jag med en kollega. Efter jobbet köpte jag mat. Klockan sex åkte jag hem. Hemma åt jag middag och pluggade svenska.

takeaways: Use one past form for every person: jag jobbade, hon jobbade, vi jobbade.
Read the present form: -ar → -ade, -er → -de (or -te after p, k, t, s, x), short verbs with a vowel + r → -dde.
Learn frequent irregular verbs as pairs: är–var, har–hade, går–gick, äter–åt, gör–gjorde.
Hem is a direction; hemma is a location. React to news before asking what happened.

pages.title: Textbook page practice: Blommor och flaskor vin
pages.intro: This diary page belongs to the textbook's own story (Nora). Use it to notice group 1 plurals (-or) and time phrases such as för två veckor sedan and en vecka senare.

recallCues: Nora met a good-looking man two weeks ago. He wrote, they agreed to meet, and yesterday he sent her a flower.

lines.fi: Jag träffade en snygg man för två veckor sedan. Förra veckan skrev han ett meddelande till mig och sa att han ville träffas. Jag svarade att vi kan träffas nästa vecka. Igår skickade han en blomma till min adress. Hur visste han att jag älskar blommor?

sections.title: Meet the five plural groups
body: Plural means two or more. English usually adds -s: one car, two cars. Swedish has five plural endings, so your teacher sorts nouns into five plural groups.
Two clues point to the group. Is the noun an en-word or an ett-word? And what is its last letter? En blomma is an en-word that ends in -a, so it is group 1: två blommor.
These are the teacher's clues, not laws. They work for many nouns, and the teacher lists the exceptions you need now. Learn every new noun as a pair: en bil, två bilar.

To count, put the number before the plural. One is en or ett, so it matches the noun: en bil, ett äpple. From two upwards, use the plural: två bilar, tre äpplen. Your textbook marks the groups too: page 22 shows group 1, page 23 groups 2 and 3.

items.why: Lampa is an en-word ending in -a: två lampor.
Stol is a short everyday en-word: två stolar.
Tidning ends in -ing: två tidningar.
Nyckel has e as its second-last letter. The e drops: två nycklar.
Tomat came into Swedish from another language: två tomater.
Servitör is a loanword, like frisör and direktör: två servitörer.
Äpple is an ett-word ending in a vowel: två äpplen.
Meddelande is an ett-word ending in a vowel: två meddelanden.
Hus is an ett-word ending in a consonant: två hus.
Läkare is a job ending in -are, so it has no plural ending: två läkare.

activity.summary: The clues work for many nouns. When you meet a new noun, check its plural in a dictionary and learn the pair.

sections.title: Groups 1 and 2: -or and -ar
body: Group 1: en-words that end in -a. Take away the -a and add -or: en blomma → blommor, en vecka → veckor, en kvinna → kvinnor, en flaska → flaskor.
Group 2 takes -ar. The teacher gives three clues. First, many short everyday en-words: en bil → bilar, en hund → hundar, en buss → bussar.

Second, en-words with e as the last or second-last letter. That e drops before -ar: en pojke → pojkar, en cykel → cyklar. Third, words that end in -ing: en tidning → tidningar, en klänning → klänningar.
The short-word clue is the weakest. Sak, katt, chef and vän look like group 2, but they take -er. You meet them in the next topic.

sections.title: Group 3 and the teacher's exceptions
body: Group 3 takes -er. The teacher's clue: words that came into Swedish from other languages (loanwords). En banan → bananer, en tomat → tomater, en apelsin → apelsiner, and job words on -ör: en frisör → frisörer, en servitör → servitörer, en ingenjör → ingenjörer, en direktör → direktörer.

You cannot always know where a word comes from, so listen to it. Many group 3 loanwords are stressed on the last syllable: ba-NAN, to-MAT, apel-SIN, fri-SÖR, bil-JETT, tele-FON. Stress at the end is a strong hint for -er.
Two ett-words also take -er: ett museum → museer (take away -um first) and ett protein → proteiner. Ett vitamin → vitaminer on page 23 works the same way.

Four short en-words look like group 2 but take -er: en sak → saker, en katt → katter, en chef → chefer, en vän → vänner. The ä in vän is short, so the n is written twice when an ending follows: vänner.
A few -er words also change their vowel: en bok → böcker, en son → söner (page 23). Learn these exceptions as whole pairs. Do not build a new rule from them.

sections.title: Groups 4 and 5: ett-words and jobs on -are
body: Group 4: ett-words that end in a vowel. Just add -n: ett möte → möten, ett äpple → äpplen, ett konto → konton, ett meddelande → meddelanden.
Group 5: ett-words that end in a consonant. Add nothing: ett jobb → två jobb, ett företag → två företag, ett barn → två barn, ett spel → två spel, ett hus → två hus.

Group 5 also has some en-words for jobs and origins. The teacher's examples end in -are: en lärare → två lärare, en läkare → två läkare, en italienare → två italienare. Here in Finland: en finländare → två finländare. Job words on -ör, like frisör, stay in group 3.
In group 5 the noun does not change, so the number or a word like många tells you it is plural: ett barn, två barn, många barn.

sections.title: Choose många or mycket
body: Use många (many) with plural things you count one by one: många bilar, många möten. Ask Hur många …? and answer with a number: Hur många bilar har ni? – Två.
Use mycket (much, a lot of) with an amount you do not count piece by piece: mycket vin, mycket kaffe, mycket tid. Ask Hur mycket …?
Pengar (money) is a plural word, but Swedish still says mycket pengar, because money is an amount. A container makes an amount countable: två flaskor vatten, tre koppar kaffe.

English a lot of fits both, and so do Hindi बहुत and Marathi खूप. Swedish makes you choose: a lot of cars is många bilar, never mycket bilar. The small words work the same way: några (some, a few) before plurals, lite (a little) before an amount: några tomater, lite mjölk.
Mycket also goes with verbs: Jag jobbar mycket (I work a lot). And inga means no before a plural: Jag har inga katter.

activity.label: Many or much?
activity.title: Count it or measure it?
activity.instructions: Choose många or mycket for each word, then say the full phrase aloud.

items.why: You can count cars: många bilar.
Coffee is an amount: mycket kaffe.

sections.title: Meet, see and play: verb pairs
body: Träffar means meet someone. A person comes after it (the object): Jag träffar Elin i kväll. Träffas means meet each other, so no person comes after it: Vi träffas i kväll. In the past: träffade and träffades.
Ser and ses work the same way: Vi ser en älg (we see a moose). Vi ses! means See you! (we will see each other).
Swedish has two verbs for play. Leker is play for children and pets: Barnen leker i trädgården. Spelar is for games, sports and instruments: Jag spelar fotboll. Alex spelar datorspel.
Lagar means repair: Han lagar cyklar. Laga mat means cook: Vi lagar mat tillsammans.

examples.fi: Jag träffar Elin i kväll.
examples.en: I am meeting Elin tonight.
examples.note: Träffar + a person.

examples.fi: Vi träffas i kväll.
examples.en: We are meeting (each other) tonight.
examples.note: Träffas: no person after it.

examples.fi: Vi träffades för två veckor sedan.
examples.en: We met two weeks ago.
examples.note: The past of träffas; för … sedan is on page 22.

assignment.title: Episode 7 mission: Things at home
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Give Elin a six-line tour of things in your home. Use at least three plural groups, one exact number, många and mycket.

WRITING: Send a shopping list and short message to a flatmate.

RETURN: Tomorrow, name five things at home from memory and give their plurals.
assignment.model: Hemma har jag tre rum. Jag har två lampor och fyra stolar. I vardagsrummet finns många böcker och två bord. Jag har också tre växter. I köket har jag många glas, men inte mycket kaffe. Jag har inga katter.

takeaways: Group 1 (-or): en-words ending in -a, en blomma → blommor. Group 2 (-ar): many short en-words, and words with e near the end or -ing, en pojke → pojkar.

Group 3 (-er): words from other languages, often stressed on the last syllable (bananer, telefoner), plus the teacher's exceptions saker, katter, chefer, vänner, museer, proteiner. Group 4 (-n): ett-words ending in a vowel. Group 5 (no ending): ett-words ending in a consonant, and jobs on -are.

Count with många (många böcker) and några; describe an amount with mycket (mycket kaffe, mycket pengar) and lite. A lot of cars = många bilar. You träffar someone, but vi träffas; children leker, and you spelar games.

Ask for at least three items with numbers or många.

sections.title: Put past events in order
body: A list becomes a story when the listener knows when things happened and in what order. Start with a time: igår (yesterday), igår kväll (last night), i morse (this morning), i lördags (last Saturday), förra veckan (last week), förra året (last year). Then guide the listener with först (first), sedan (then), efter det (after that) and till slut (finally). In speech, sedan is often said sen.

Swedish keeps the verb in the second position. When a time phrase or a signpost takes the first place, the past-tense verb comes next and the subject follows: Förra veckan läste vi en bok. English says “Last week we read”, so English speakers often write Förra veckan vi läste. That is the most common mistake here. Put the verb straight after the first phrase.
To say ago, wrap the time between för and sedan: för en månad sedan (a month ago), för två dagar sedan (two days ago). English puts ago only at the end; Swedish needs both words.

Började works like a modal verb: the next verb stays in the infinitive. Jag började skriva. Jag började att skriva is also correct. Att before an action means to: Jag gillar att dansa. Before a whole statement it means that: Jag berättade att jag var trött.

examples.fi: Igår spelade jag datorspel.
examples.en: Yesterday I played video games.
examples.note: Igår first; spelade second; jag third.

examples.fi: Igår kväll beställde jag en pizza.
examples.en: Last night I ordered a pizza.
examples.note: The whole time phrase igår kväll fills the first place.

examples.fi: Först åt jag fattiga riddare till frukost. Sedan gick jag på bio. Efter det träffade jag en vän.
examples.en: First I ate French toast for breakfast. Then I went to the cinema. After that I met a friend.
examples.note: Three signposts make the order clear. Fattiga riddare (poor knights) is the Swedish name for French toast.

examples.fi: Jag reste till Spanien för ett år sedan.
examples.en: I travelled to Spain a year ago.
examples.note: För … sedan wraps the time.

examples.fi: En kaka köpte hon igår.
examples.en: She bought a cake yesterday (a cake, not bread).
examples.note: The teacher also starts with an object, the thing the action affects, to stress it. The verb still comes second.

sections.memoryTip: TIME → VERB → PERSON: Förra veckan → läste → vi. The verb never waits in third place.
sections.tryIt: Say three true or invented events from yesterday. Begin each line with Igår, Sedan or Efter det, and put the verb next.

activity.label: Verb second?
activity.title: Is the verb in the second place?
activity.instructions: Read each line and predict: is it correct Swedish, or does the verb come too late? Then say the correct version aloud.

items.why: Igår takes the first place, so the verb comes next: Igår spelade jag datorspel.

items.fi: Förra veckan läste vi en bok.
items.en: Last week we read a book.
items.why: Förra veckan, then läste, then vi.

items.en: Then we went to the cinema.
items.why: Sedan is a signpost in the first place: Sedan gick vi på bio.

items.fi: Igår kväll beställde jag en pizza.
items.en: Last night I ordered a pizza.
items.why: Igår kväll is one time phrase, so beställde is still second.

items.fi: Jag reste till Spanien förra året.
items.en: I travelled to Spain last year.
items.why: The subject jag is first, so reste is second. The time can also come at the end.

items.fi: I morse jag tränade på gymmet.
items.en: This morning I worked out at the gym.
items.why: After I morse the verb comes next: I morse tränade jag på gymmet.
The object en kaka is first, and köpte is still second.
Till slut takes the first place: Till slut gick jag hem.

activity.summary: Whatever comes first, the verb comes next.

sections.title: Write to a friend
body: An informal letter or message sounds like a conversation. It has four parts: a greeting with your friend's name (Hej Elin!), your news in time order, one real question so your friend can answer, and a warm closing such as Kram, Vi ses or Vi hörs, with your name.
After the greeting, a short friendly question is natural: Hur är det med dig? or Hur mår du? Then tell your news with time words and signposts. Short and correct is better than long and unsure.

A diary is for yourself and a letter is for another person, but both often begin with a date: den 4 maj. Read it aloud with an ordinal number, a counting word for order: den fjärde maj. You will practise more ordinals in Lecture 10.
The YKI basic-level writing test has this kind of task: a short card or message to a friend, with a list of points to cover. You must open and close it in a suitable way and cover every point.

sections.title: Say what it is about
body: Use handlar om to name the topic of a book, film, letter or conversation: Filmen handlar om vänskap. Learn it as one chunk.
Do not translate English word for word. Swedish does not say Filmen är om vänskap. Say Filmen handlar om vänskap.
In a question, om moves to the end: Vad handlar filmen om? (What is the film about?)
Without om, handla is a different verb: it means to shop. Vi handlade mat means We bought food. Listen for om to know which one you hear.

examples.fi: Filmen handlar om vänskap.
examples.en: The film is about friendship.

examples.fi: Boken handlar om Finland.
examples.en: The book is about Finland.

examples.fi: Vad handlar boken om?
examples.en: What is the book about?
examples.note: In a question, om goes to the end.

examples.fi: Jag har något viktigt att berätta. Det handlar om jobbet.
examples.en: I have something important to tell you. It is about work.
examples.note: A useful way to start news in a letter.

examples.fi: I lördags handlade vi mat.
examples.en: On Saturday we bought food.
examples.note: No om: handla means to shop.

sections.memoryTip: THING + handlar om + TOPIC. Question: Vad handlar den om? No om = shopping.
sections.tryIt: Name one film or book you like and say what it is about. Then ask: Vad handlar din favoritfilm om?

activity.label: About or shopping?
activity.title: Which handla is it?
activity.instructions: Decide what handlar means in each line. Look for om. Then say the line aloud.

items.fi: Filmen handlar om två gamla vänner.
items.why: Handlar om + topic: the film is about two old friends.
No om after handlade, and mat is what they bought.
Om sits at the end of the question: What is the letter about?

items.fi: Jag handlar i en mataffär nära jobbet.
items.why: I en mataffär tells where you shop: I shop at a grocery shop near work.
Handlar om + Finland: the book is about Finland.
No om after handlade, and kläder is what she bought.

activity.summary: Handlar om + topic means is about. Handla without om means to shop.

sections.title: Small words after verbs
body: Some Swedish verbs and adjectives always take a small word after them, a preposition. It is often not the one English uses, so learn the pair as one chunk.
Waiting and many feelings take på: vänta på (wait for), arg på (angry with), besviken på (disappointed in). Being in love takes i: kär i.
Berätta has two partners: berätta om something (tell about it) and berätta för someone (tell it to them): Jag berättade om helgen för Elin.

examples.fi: Jag väntade på bussen i tjugo minuter.
examples.en: I waited for the bus for twenty minutes.
examples.note: English for, Swedish på.

examples.fi: Bli inte arg på mig!
examples.en: Do not be angry with me!
examples.note: English with, Swedish på.

examples.fi: Jag var besviken på filmen.
examples.en: I was disappointed in the film.

examples.fi: Elin är kär i Mikko.
examples.en: Elin is in love with Mikko.
examples.note: English with, Swedish i.

examples.fi: Jag berättade om helgen för Elin.
examples.en: I told Elin about the weekend.
examples.note: om = about; för = to the person.

sections.memoryTip: English for, with, in → Swedish often på: vänta på, arg på, besviken på.
sections.tryIt: Say one true sentence with vänta på and one with berätta för.
